items.body_md:
On August 18, the publishers filed five reply briefs in support of their motions to exclude Anthropic's expert witnesses, completing the Daubert briefing cycle in No. 5:24-cv-03811 ahead of the October 21 summary judgment hearing before Judge Eumi K. Lee.

Dkt. 766 is the only publicly captioned entry in yesterday's cluster: the publishers' reply in support of their motion to partially exclude Dr. Abhishek Nagaraj (Dkt. 650), filed by counsel Bret Matera on behalf of all plaintiff entities — Concord Music Group, ABKCO Music, Capitol CMG, Polygram Publishing, Songs of Universal, Universal Music Corp., Universal Music-MGB NA, and Universal Music-Z Tunes. The remaining four replies (Dkts. 768, 770, 773, 776), each accompanied by a supporting declaration and one or more sealed exhibits (Dkts. 767, 769, 771-772, 774-775, 778, 780), mirror the same filing architecture and almost certainly carry the publishers' final words on the motions to exclude Anthropic's other disclosed experts — Dr. Andrew Bray, Dr. Jeffrey Bilmes, and Dr. Russ Altman — whose motions in limine were filed March 31 and opposed by Anthropic on July 27 (Dkts. 748, 750, 752). A fifth reply (Dkt. 781) and its sealed companion (Dkt. 780) follow the same pattern; the Colin E. Stokes motion in limine filed in the same March 31 tranche is the likeliest candidate for that slot, though the public docket caption is sealed. With yesterday's filings, every Daubert motion is now fully briefed on both sides.

The strategic weight here is straightforward: the publishers are asking Judge Lee to exclude the expert testimony Anthropic intends to rely on at the summary judgment hearing and, if the case reaches trial, before a jury. Dr. Nagaraj is understood to be Anthropic's damages or market-harm expert; Dr. Bilmes and Dr. Altman bear on technical AI questions central to the fair use analysis; Dr. Bray addresses statistical or quantitative issues in the publishers' evidence. Successful exclusion of any of these witnesses would narrow what Anthropic can argue on fair use — particularly the "transformative use" and market-harm factors that are the center of gravity on both summary judgment motions. The sealed exhibits across Dkts. 767-780 are almost certainly the deposition excerpts and technical materials the publishers marshaled in their reply; their content is not publicly available. The next concrete event is the September 2 Case Management Conference before Judge Lee (videoconference, 4:00 PM PT), where the court will likely address any remaining scheduling or sequencing questions ahead of October 21.

items.body_md:
On August 17, the publishers filed their Responsive Separate Statement (Dkt. 756) together with a supporting declaration (Dkt. 757), a notice (Dkt. 758), and two documents under seal (Dkts. 759–760), completing the publishers' opposition-side factual record on the cross-motions for summary judgment before Judge Eumi K. Lee in No. 5:24-cv-03811. The Responsive Separate Statement is the publishers' point-by-point answer to Anthropic's separate statement of undisputed facts — the document that locks in which material facts the publishers dispute, on what evidentiary basis, and where genuine issues of fact exist that the court must resolve before it can grant or deny either side's motion. Because the summary judgment hearing is set for October 21, this filing completes the factual-dispute record that Judge Lee will have in front of her; it is not a preliminary skirmish.

The sealed companion filings (Dkts. 759–760) almost certainly carry the underlying exhibits the declaration references — consistent with the pattern set by the July 27 round of sealed Daubert oppositions (Dkts. 745–753), where substantive evidence was filed under the standing sealing order (Dkt. 590). The content is not publicly available, but the structure of the filing cluster mirrors prior sealed merits submissions in this case. What matters for recovery posture is the scope of what the publishers chose to contest: a narrow responsive statement, accepting most of Anthropic's facts, would signal confidence that disputed facts alone carry their partial summary judgment motion on direct infringement; a broad one, contesting the bulk of Anthropic's statement, signals that the publishers view the factual record as genuinely contested on fair use and may be laying the foundation for a trial rather than a clean pre-trial adjudication. That distinction cannot be assessed until the sealed exhibits surface or the court rules.


The publishers have narrowed Concord I to direct infringement and alleged removal of copyright management information, having dropped earlier contributory and vicarious infringement claims.
 The summary judgment motion accordingly turns on whether Anthropic's training use was fair use — 
Anthropic argues the use was "transformative" fair use analogous to how humans learn from reading, while the publishers counter that Anthropic used the lyrics to build a competing commercial product and fair use does not apply.
 Running in parallel, 
Anthropic and Dario Amodei have each filed dismissal motions in Concord II targeting the case covering more than 20,000 songs, with Anthropic seeking to strike the output-reproduction claim and a DMCA count.
 The November 4 hearing on those partial motions to dismiss in No. 5:26-cv-00880 is the next inflection point for the broader multi-suit exposure picture. The next concrete milestone in Concord I is the September 2 Case Management Conference before Judge Lee, followed by the October 21 summary judgment hearing.

items.body_md:
The press coverage that landed August 5–6 fills in the structural detail on Anthropic's Concord II partial dismissal motions that yesterday's edition flagged at the level of their existence and general thrust. The more precise picture, now confirmed across multiple sources, is that Anthropic is not seeking to dismiss the core torrenting and training allegations — those remain live — but is instead targeting two specific, downstream claims: the output-based infringement count, and a Digital Millennium Copyright Act count. 
Anthropic argued that the complaint, covering roughly 21,000 works, never cites one instance of Claude reproducing a lyric, and asked that the output claim be dismissed with prejudice.
 The "with prejudice" ask is the sharpest edge here: if granted, the publishers would be barred from replying that claim in its current form, eliminating what would otherwise be the most direct mechanism to show consumer-facing harm at trial. 
Anthropic also moved to dismiss the DMCA count, arguing the statute reaches only the stripping of copyright management information from a complete work, and that the publishers never allege Anthropic held their full compositions.
 That DMCA theory, if it had survived, would have provided a separate damages floor independent of statutory copyright damages — its loss narrows the publishers' damages architecture in Concord II, though it has no direct bearing on the infringement claims already advancing in 5:24-cv-03811. 
The two filings landed on Monday, August 3, in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California.



Concord II carries case number 5:26-cv-00880, was filed January 28, 2026, and names Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and co-founder Benjamin Mann as individual defendants
 — the confirmed case number is worth logging cleanly given the parallel docket management now running alongside 5:24-cv-03811. 
Amodei filed separately to get the direct infringement count against him personally dropped; Anthropic did not move against the torrenting and training claims, which it continues to contest.
 The strategic implication for rights-holders in both proceedings is that Anthropic has chosen to fight the input-side allegations on the merits while attempting to clear the output-side and DMCA theories at the pleading stage — a posture that, if successful, would concentrate the entire evidentiary burden of the litigation on the training-data conduct and away from anything Claude does in response to user prompts. Whether the publishers can amend to supply the missing output examples, or whether the court grants dismissal with prejudice on that count, will materially affect the damages ceiling they can present to any jury in Concord II.

Nothing new has landed on the Concord I docket (5:24-cv-03811) since yesterday's edition. The next concrete event remains the Case Management Conference before Judge Lee on Zoom on September 2, 2026, followed by the Summary Judgment Hearing on October 21, 2026 — at which the fair use and direct infringement questions in the original case will be the focus. The Concord II partial dismissal argument on November 4 then follows, meaning Judge Lee will have issued her summary judgment ruling in Concord I, or will be close to doing so, at the point she hears the threshold pleading challenges in Concord II. That sequencing matters: a summary judgment ruling adverse to Anthropic on training-data fair use in Concord I would substantially undercut the legal premise of the same argument Anthropic is mounting in Concord II.
